890.title: The development of doctrine
890.hook: Newman: living ideas grow like a tree, staying themselves
890.howItsDone: Catholic theologians and teachers draw on Newman's idea of development when they explain how the Church's teaching is put into new words over the centuries while remaining faithful to what was handed down.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Henry Newman, later a priest of the Oratory, on a ship with no wind. Your line was lead, kindly light. Today, the question Newman was wrestling with when he turned.

An old photograph: a child on a doorstep, gap-toothed, in a too-big sweater. Then the same person decades later. The height, the face, the voice, all different. And yet nobody at the family table doubts it's the same person. Something stayed while everything grew. Newman put a question like that to the whole Church. The first Christians didn't use every word the Church uses now. So is today's Church a different thing wearing an old name? Or the same thing, grown up?
screen: `A CHILD, THEN A GROWN ADULT.` → `THE SAME PERSON?` → `THE SAME CHURCH?`

segments.voice: Newman wrote a long book about it, An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, in the months before he became Catholic. First, the problem. Some teachings were said in words the first Christians never used. The creed says the Son is of one substance with the Father, a phrase that isn't in the Gospels. Did the Church add something new, or put into words what was there all along? Second, the image. A living idea, Newman argued, grows the way living things grow: a seed becomes a tree. Jesus himself compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds come to rest. The tree looks nothing like the seed, yet it is the same plant, and no other plant could come from that seed. Third, the sentence. Newman wrote: "In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often." It does not say anything goes. Fourth, the test. Ideas can also decay, the way a body can sicken instead of grow. So Newman tried to describe how to tell a true development from a corruption: a true one keeps the same type and principles, and carries forward what came before instead of overturning it. Catholic teaching today speaks of doctrine developing in this sense. Other Christians describe faithfulness over time in their own ways. For Newman, the question was not whether the Church had changed. It was whether it had stayed itself while growing.
screen: `WORDS THE FIRST CHRISTIANS NEVER USED.` · `A SEED BECOMES A TREE.` · `HERE BELOW TO LIVE IS TO CHANGE.` · `GROWTH, OR DECAY?` · then, large: `TO BE PERFECT IS TO HAVE CHANGED OFTEN.`

segments.voice: Think back to how you understood God, or goodness, or what matters, as a child, a picture, a prayer, a rule, and set it next to how you understand it today. What has changed, and what, under all that change, has stayed the same? If you pray, give thanks for the growth; if you don't, notice the thread that runs from then to now.
Mustard seed. The image Jesus used for a growing kingdom, which Newman borrowed to explain how a true teaching can grow into something unrecognizable and still be the same plant.
Your line: to live is to change. The seed and the tree are one plant. Eight hundred ninety days now.

891.title: Bernadette in the convent
891.hook: asked about Lourdes, she says she was used like a broom and put back
891.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Bernadette's feast in April, and pilgrims to Lourdes often also visit the convent chapel at Nevers, where her body lies in a glass reliquary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Newman's idea of doctrine growing like a mustard seed into a tree. Your line was to live is to change. Today, a girl from Lourdes, years later.

A visitor at a convent door in Nevers, in the middle of France, hopes for a glimpse of the famous one. Back in Lourdes, the grotto where she knelt is drawing crowds, a church is rising above it, and the sick are coming to the spring. Here, far to the north, the girl at the center of it all is sweeping, folding linen, helping in the infirmary, and often sick in bed herself. When people press her about what she saw, she gives an answer that sounds almost like a joke. It is about a broom.
screen: `A CONVENT IN NEVERS.` → `CROWDS AT THE GROTTO.` → `SHE TALKS ABOUT A BROOM.`

segments.voice: Bernadette Soubirous, the girl who said a lady appeared to her at the grotto of Lourdes, did not stay in Lourdes. She joined the Sisters of Charity of Nevers and left her home town for their mother house. First, leaving. At Lourdes she could not walk down a street without being stared at, questioned, asked to touch rosaries. In the convent she asked to be one sister among many. Second, the broom. Her fellow sisters remembered her saying something like this: the Virgin used me like a broom; when you've finished sweeping, you put the broom back in its place, in the corner, behind the door. That's where I am now. She did not see herself as the point of the story. The lady was, and the message. She was the tool, and the tool had been put away. Third, the sickbed. She was often ill, for long stretches, and tradition remembers her calling illness her work. She helped as a nurse's aide and in the sacristy when she was able. Some of the sisters in charge were hard on her, and she bore it quietly. Fourth, why she is a saint. The Church canonized her for how she lived, not simply for what she reported seeing. Mary's own song in Luke's Gospel says it in the Douay-Rheims: "Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid." Regarded. Seen. Bernadette's holiness, in the Church's eyes, was mostly hidden, in a convent, in a sickbed, like a broom behind the door.
screen: `SHE LEAVES LOURDES FOR NEVERS.` · `A BROOM, PUT BACK IN ITS PLACE.` · `ILLNESS AS HER WORK.` · `A SAINT FOR HOW SHE LIVED.` · then, large: `THE HUMILITY OF HIS HANDMAID.`

892.title: Damien of Molokai (1840–1889)
892.hook: a Belgian priest serves the leprosy settlement on Molokai and, tradition says, begins his sermons we lepers
892.howItsDone: Catholics in Hawaii keep Saint Damien's feast on May 10, and parishes and shrines named for him remember him as a friend of people with Hansen's disease.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernadette Soubirous in the convent, the broom after the sweeping. Your line was put back in the corner. Today, a priest who went where people were sent away.

On the island of Molokai, in Hawaii, a flat green peninsula sits at the foot of tall sea cliffs: sea in front, a wall of rock behind. The Hawaiian kingdom sent people with leprosy there, by law, to live apart. Families were split on the docks, and those sent were not expected back. A young priest from Belgium, already working on the islands, offers to go. He lands with very little. Tradition says that for years his sermons began my brethren. Then, one Sunday, they began with two different words.
screen: `A PENINSULA UNDER THE CLIFFS.` → `SENT AWAY, BY LAW.` → `A PRIEST OFFERS TO GO.`

segments.voice: His name was Jozef De Veuster. In religious life he took the name Damien, as a member of the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts. The Church now calls him Saint Damien of Molokai. First, the work. The settlement on the Kalaupapa peninsula needed everything. Damien dressed wounds, built houses and helped build a church. He dug graves and made coffins, so the dying could be buried with dignity. He organized care for orphaned children. Second, the nearness. He did not keep a careful distance. He ate with the people, shared his pipe, touched the sick. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus describes the Son of man welcoming those who cared for him: "sick, and you visited me." In the Latin of the Vulgate, sick is infirmus. Damien took the visiting part to its end. Third, the two words. In time Damien found that he had the disease himself. Tradition says that from then on, he began his sermons not my brethren, but we lepers. No longer one who visits. One of them. Fourth, the end. He kept working as long as he could, and died on Molokai, among the people he had come to serve. A word about the word. Leprosy is what the disease was called then, and it is in the saint's own sentence. Today it is called Hansen's disease, and it can be cured. Some people who have lived with it have asked not to be called lepers, and his line is honored as his, not as a label for anyone else.
screen: `DRESSING WOUNDS, BUILDING COFFINS.` · `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.` · `FROM MY BRETHREN TO WE LEPERS.` · `HE DIED AMONG THEM.` · then, large: `WE LEPERS.`

segments.voice: Who is sent to the edge where you live: someone sick, someone old and alone, someone everyone avoids? If you pray, pray for that person by name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.

893.title: Marianne Cope (1838–1918)
893.hook: a German-American sister who went to nurse in Hawaii and, the accounts of her life say, stayed thirty years at Molokai
893.howItsDone: Catholics in Hawaii and in Syracuse, New York, keep Saint Marianne Cope's feast on January 23, and Catholic hospitals and nurses often remember her as an example of care for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Damien of Molokai on the Kalaupapa peninsula, and the two words that began his sermons. Your line was we lepers. Today, the woman who cared for Damien himself.

Hungry for the work. Those are the words a convent superior in Syracuse, New York, writes back to Hawaii. A priest there is looking for sisters to nurse people with leprosy. He has asked community after community, and they have said no. She has a hospital to run in New York, sisters who rely on her, a life full of work already. Still, she answers that she wants to go, and that she wishes with all her heart to be one of the chosen ones.
screen: `HUNGRY FOR THE WORK.` → `OTHERS HAVE SAID NO.` → `SHE WANTS TO GO.`

segments.voice: Her name was Marianne Cope, a Franciscan sister. The Church now calls her Saint Marianne of Molokai. First, the immigrant girl. She was born in Germany, and her family came to New York state when she was small. As a young woman she worked in a factory to help support them, and only later could she enter religious life. Second, the hospital builder. In Syracuse and Utica her community opened hospitals, and she helped run them. They took in patients other hospitals turned away. She learned how to organize care, keep a ward clean, and stand up for the sick. Third, Hawaii. She sailed with a small group of sisters, nursed first in Honolulu, and then went to Kalaupapa on Molokai. She arrived as Father Damien was dying. She nursed him, and after his death she took over the care of the boys he had looked after. She ran a new home for women and girls, and insisted on cleanliness, on gardens, on pretty things like flowers and ribbons, so that a place of exile could feel like a home. Fourth, the staying. The accounts of her life say she stayed thirty years at Molokai, and she died there. She did not go back to New York. Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." Damien carried the people of Kalaupapa. Marianne carried Damien, and then his work. The caregiver was cared for.

894.title: John Bosco (1815–1888)
894.hook: a priest who took in street boys and taught through games and kindness
894.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint John Bosco's feast on January 31, and Salesian schools and youth centers often mark it with Mass, games and a festival for their students.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marianne Cope, who nursed Damien and carried on his work. Your line was she stayed thirty years. Today, a priest with a rope stretched between two trees.

A farm boy in the hills of Piedmont, in northern Italy, has been watching the traveling acrobats at the village fairs. He goes home and practices: juggling, conjuring tricks, walking on a rope tied between two trees. Before long the other children gather to watch. And this is the deal, as he later told it in his memoirs: the show is free, but it comes with a prayer, and with the morning's sermon, repeated from memory. The boy grew up to be a priest in Turin, and he kept the same instinct. Start where young people already are.
screen: `A BOY ON A ROPE.` → `A FREE SHOW, AND A PRAYER.` → `START WHERE THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: His name was John Bosco, Don Bosco in Italian. First, the city. Turin was growing fast, full of factories and building sites. Boys came in from the countryside looking for work and ended up on the streets, some in prison. Don Bosco visited the prisons and was struck by how young the prisoners were. He wanted to reach boys before they ended up there. Second, the oratory. He gathered them on Sundays, in fields and yards at first, for games, Mass, catechism and food. Over time it became a home, with a roof, beds, workshops where boys learned trades, and schools. Third, the method. He called it the preventive system, summed up in three words usually translated reason, religion and loving-kindness. Reason: explain, don't just command. Religion: the sacraments and prayer at the center. Loving-kindness: the boys had to be able to tell that they were loved. In a letter from Rome he wrote, in effect, that it is not enough to love the young; they must know they are loved. Paul says it in his first letter to the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Charity is patient, is kind." Fourth, the family he left. To keep the work going, he founded the Salesians, named for Saint Francis de Sales, a gentle bishop, and with Saint Mary Mazzarello a community of sisters for girls. The Salesians still run schools and youth centers, and the playground is still part of the plan. A priest who once walked a rope to win a crowd never stopped believing that games could be holy ground.

895.title: Rerum Novarum (1891)
895.hook: Leo XIII writes on workers: fair wages, unions and dignity
895.howItsDone: Catholic parishes, schools and charities draw on the Church's social teaching in their work for fair wages, housing and the poor, and on May 1 the Church keeps the memorial of Saint Joseph the Worker.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Bosco and the boys of Turin. Your line was reason, faith, kindness. Today, a pope writes about the factory floor.

A factory whistle before sunrise. Men, women and children walk in through the gate, and they will not walk out until dark. The pay barely covers bread and rent. If someone is hurt at the machine, there is often no help and no job tomorrow. In the cities of the new industrial age, people argued hard about what to do. Some said the owners owed nothing beyond the agreed wage. Others said the whole system should be torn down. Then a pope, Leo the Thirteenth, sent a letter to the bishops of the world, and it was about workers.
screen: `A FACTORY WHISTLE BEFORE DAWN.` → `TWO LOUD ANSWERS.` → `A POPE WRITES ABOUT WORKERS.`

segments.voice: Papal letters like this are called encyclicals, named for their first words in Latin. This one begins Rerum novarum, of new things. In Latin the phrase also meant upheaval, even revolution, and the letter opens on that restless spirit of change: new industries, great wealth for a few, a new kind of poverty for many. Leo makes four arguments. First, the worker is a person. Employers must not treat workers as slaves or as tools, and must respect their dignity as human beings. Second, a just wage. An agreement about pay is not automatically fair just because both sides signed it. A wage must be enough to support a worker who lives simply and works honestly. If hunger forces a man to accept less, that is injustice, even if it is a contract. Jesus says it plainly in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "for the labourer is worthy of his hire." Third, unions. Leo defends the right of workers to form associations, to band together for their own good. Fourth, no class war. Leo also defends private property, and rejects the idea that owners and workers are natural enemies. Each has duties to the other, he says, and the state has a duty to protect the weakest. That gives today's word, social teaching: the body of the Church's teaching about how a society should be ordered, on work, wages, property, the poor, the common good. Later popes kept returning to Rerum Novarum and building on it. Leo's answer, in the end, was that the person at the machine matters more than the machine.

896.title: The Uganda martyrs (1886)
896.hook: Charles Lwanga and young companions, Catholic and Anglican, killed by a king
896.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Charles Lwanga and companions on June 3, and on that day pilgrims from Uganda and neighboring countries gather at the Catholic and Anglican shrines at Namugongo.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rerum Novarum and the Church's social teaching. Your line was the dignity of work. Today, young men at a royal court, and the end of a week.

The court of the Kabaka, the king of Buganda, on the shores of a great lake in East Africa. Young pages run messages, carry water, stand at the doors. Some of them have been listening to newcomers: Catholic missionaries, and Anglican missionaries too. Some of the pages have been baptized, and they pray together in secret. The young king, Mwanga, grows angry and afraid. He sees the new faith pulling his pages' loyalty somewhere he can't control, and they are refusing some of his demands. One day he orders the Christians at court to step forward. They step forward.
screen: `THE COURT OF THE KABAKA.` → `PAGES WHO PRAY IN SECRET.` → `THE CHRISTIANS STEP FORWARD.`

segments.voice: First, the elder. Joseph Mukasa, a Catholic and a senior servant at court, had protected the pages and spoken honestly to the king. The king had him killed before the pages were taken. Second, the leader of the pages. Charles Lwanga took his place, looking after the young Christians. Tradition says that on the night before they were taken, he baptized some of the boys still waiting for baptism, so they would not die without it. Then they were marched to Namugongo, and there they were burned. Tradition remembers that they went praying, some of them singing. A boy named Kizito is remembered holding Lwanga's hand. Third, together. Anglican Christians at court died too, in the same persecution, for the same refusal. The Catholic Church has canonized Charles Lwanga and his Catholic companions, and the Church of Uganda honors its Anglican martyrs. At Namugongo there are two shrines, one Catholic and one Anglican, and pilgrims come to both. Fourth, the word martyr. It comes from the Greek for witness: someone whose life, and death, tells the truth about what they believe. Jesus says in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Look back over this week: a doctrine that grows, a broom in the corner, we lepers, a nurse who stayed, a priest on a rope, a pope on wages, and now young men from two churches walking the same road to Namugongo.
screen: `JOSEPH MUKASA, THE ELDER.` · `CHARLES LWANGA AND THE PAGES.` · `CATHOLIC AND ANGLICAN, TOGETHER.` · `MARTYR MEANS WITNESS.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT SUFFER PERSECUTION.`

segments.voice: Picture Namugongo today: two shrines, crowds of pilgrims walking the roads to get there. Think of the people of Uganda now, families, schools, churches of more than one kind, people of other faiths and of none. If you pray, pray for the country and its people; if you don't, hold them in mind with good will.
